# Proverbs 15: Research Notes

**A note on gaps:** I didn't reach any Catholic or Orthodox site (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org directly. NET Bible notes appear below only where preceptaustin.org quotes them. I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those headings are left out. Much of what passes for "Catholic" material below comes from Latin Vulgate readings and Church Fathers cited by the Pulpit Commentary, not from Catholic sources themselves.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: a gentle answer has no sharp edges and can actually turn wrath away. When people come to us in wrath, we are often tempted to be harsh in response. Wisdom shows us the value of a soft answer, one without sharp edges or points. He uses Gideon and Jephthah as his examples (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/).
- Gill: gentle words calm a person's anger so high winds are sometimes laid by soft showers. His examples are Gideon and Abigail (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/15-1.htm).
- Pulpit Commentary: two lessons here. An answer should be given - the injured person should not wrap himself in sullen silence; and that answer should be gentle and conciliatory. (same URL)
- A limit on the promise, quoted on preceptaustin: I may not assume that a soft answer will always turn away wrath. Under some circumstances it may, even at the time, have proved an additional provocation, though in the end its virtue will be acknowledged. But its tendency is to soothe and heal (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).

**v. 2**
- Ellicott says "uses knowledge aright" means the wise person brings it forth at the proper time and place. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm)
- Wesley: "pours out" means plentifully, continually, and vehemently, as a fountain does waters. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- Guzik: It isn't enough for a man or woman to claim they have wisdom in their heart or mind; what they say proves either their wisdom or folly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Constable (on preceptaustin): the contrast isn't about how much each person talks. The wise man considers what he says before he says it, but the fool does not. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary)

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: God is waiting till the iniquity of the one is full (Genesis 15:16), watching to aid the other (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Guzik: Among men, evil is often unpunished and good is often unrewarded – but God sees and notes all. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Pulpit Commentary: the verse stresses that the covenant God is everywhere and knows everything. It notes that God's name keeps recurring in this chapter and the next (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).
- Chuck Smith takes up the objection that God is too holy to look on evil. His answer: God can't look on sin with approval, But He surely sees it. He's not blind. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/15-11.html)

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: a "wholesome tongue" is one which heals and soothes by its gentleness and judicious words. A "breach in the spirit" means it deeply wounds another's spirit. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm)
- Wesley thinks the harm and the good reach both sides. Perverse speech disturbs and wounds the spirits, both of the speaker and hearers, and a wholesome tongue helps promote the spiritual and eternal life, both of the speaker and hearers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/proverbs/15.htm)
- Matthew Henry: Hard words indeed break no bones, but many a heart has been broken by them. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_015.cfm)

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Learning wisdom is more than learning facts; it is to receive correction. If what we learn only confirms what we already know, it probably isn't wisdom we are learning. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Gill (on preceptaustin): rejecting a father's instruction is not only a contempt of his authority, but a slight of his love (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: there is treasure because God's blessing is on the house. The wicked, by chasing gain recklessly, bring trouble on themselves and their families (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Guzik on whether the treasure is money: Because wisdom and godliness tend to bring prosperity, this is generally true of material treasure. Thankfully, the treasure in the house of the righteous isn't only material; the greater treasure is spiritual. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Lawson (on preceptaustin) is more cautious: some of those who are rich in faith, have no silver and gold. He reads verses 16–17 as Solomon's own explanation of this verse (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).
- Pulpit Commentary: whether the good man's store is large or small, God blesses it, so it is safe and enough (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 7**
- Wesley: "disperse" means freely communicate to others what they know. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- Another reading of the second line: Ellicott gives "Or, disperseth that which is not right." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm). The Pulpit Commentary follows Delitzsch and others in reading the Hebrew word as "right" here (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 8** (a real disagreement between traditions)
- The traditional reading is that worship without obedience is worthless. Guzik points to 1 Samuel 15:22 (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/). Ellicott says people tend to think that whatever costs them effort must please God, even when not accompanied with what alone He cares for, a loving heart. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm)
- Gill (Reformed Baptist) narrows the target to sacrifices offered without faith in Christ, without any sense of sin, repentance for it, and reformation from it (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).
- Wesley (Methodist) applies "sacrifice" to all the religious services, yea, the most costly; one kind being put for all the rest. Prayer - The cheapest and meanest services. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/proverbs/15.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) records two historical disputes over this verse:
  - The Donatists used it to argue that baptism by heretics was invalid. Augustine answered that a sacrament's validity rests on Christ's appointment, not the minister's spiritual state.
  - Others used it to argue that everything an unjustified person does is sin. Pulpit disagrees: The truer view is that God's grace does act beyond the limits of his visible Church.
  
  (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm)

**v. 9**
- NET note (on preceptaustin): the verb for "pursue" signals persistent pursuit (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).
- Pulpit Commentary: this verse explains verse 8. "Followeth after" means chaseth, implying effort and perseverance, as in the pursuit of game (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).
- Guzik: if God rejects the worship of the wicked, he rejects their sinful way of life even more (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/).

**v. 10**
- Ellicott and Pulpit both prefer the translation "there is a grievous correction for him that forsaketh the way." Ellicott describes punishment meant to correct first, and finally death for those who stubbornly hate reproof (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Guzik: the harsh discipline is God's mercy, a warning and opportunity to change one's ways. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- NET note (on preceptaustin): the Hebrew for "severe discipline" indicates a discipline that is catastrophic or harmful to life. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary)
- A doctrinal point specific to preceptaustin: the page reads "forsakes" as close to apostasy, but adds that true believers may have moments (even seasons) of backsliding, but they will always endure the end. That is a perseverance-of-the-saints reading (same URL). Guzik quotes Waltke saying "will die" means eternal death (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/).

**v. 11**
- Pulpit Commentary: Sheol is the receptacle of all departed spirits, whether good or bad. Abaddon is the lowest depth of hell. The argument runs from the greater to the lesser: if God sees the world beyond the grave, he certainly sees human thoughts (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/15-11.htm).
- Ellicott: Abaddon is the abode of evil spirits and the lost. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm)
- Other readings:
  - The Bible Hub study notes describe Sheol as a shadowy underworld, distinct from the concept of hell in later Christian theology. (https://biblehub.com/proverbs/15-11.htm)
  - Coffman says Abaddon, like Sheol, is a place name for the realm of the dead.
  - Matthew Henry notes Abaddon is also one of the devil's names (Revelation 9:11).
  
  (Coffman and Henry: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/15-11.html)

**v. 12**
- Matthew Henry gives two senses. The scorner won't let his own conscience correct him, and he will not go unto the wise, lest they should give him wise counsel. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_015.cfm)
- Pulpit Commentary: scorners are conceited, sceptical people, too sure of their own opinions to take advice (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 13**
- Pulpit Commentary: happiness shows on the face, but sorrow goes deeper. It reaches the inner life and leads to despondency (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).
- Guzik quotes Bridges: this cheerfulness is not the noisy mirth of the ungodly (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/).

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the wise become wiser and fools become more foolish. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Wesley: Wickedness is meat and drink to them. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- Gill applies the verse to foolish and false doctrines and calls all unregenerate people such fools (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-15.html).

**v. 15** (interpreters disagree on who "the oppressed" are)
- Gloomy in mind: Ellicott says it is not one who has to bear great misfortunes, but one who makes the worst of everything (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm). Pulpit limits it to mental, not material, trouble and says the Vulgate's "the poor" gives the wrong impression (https://biblehub.com/proverbs/15-15.htm). Wesley: Of the troubled in mind. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- Truly afflicted: Gill takes it of people who suffer all their lives, like Jacob. He also mentions the rendering "the poor." He finds the "continual feast" in a heart where God's kingdom dwells (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/15-15.htm).
- Waltke (on preceptaustin): people who really are afflicted can still have the cheerful heart that helps them overcome (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).
- Early Latin reading: the Vulgate has "a secure mind is like a perpetual feast," and Pulpit cites Gregory the Great on it (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 16**
- Gill: this is not that a "little" is better than "much" of that which is good... poverty is not better than riches, simply considered. The point is the good man's little (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/15-16.htm).
- Wesley defines the "trouble": Tumultuous lusts and passions, vexatious cares, and horrors of conscience. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- POSB (on preceptaustin): the word for "trouble" mostly means turmoil sent by God in judgment (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).

**v. 17**
- Matthew Henry: when family members live together in love, it makes a dinner of herbs a feast sufficient (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/15-16.html).
- Bridges (on preceptaustin) treats verses 16–17 together as the sources of a cheerful heart: the fear of the LORD and the love of man. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary)

**v. 18**
- Gill: the hot-tempered man stirs up strife as a man stirs up coals of fire and raises a flame (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-15.html).
- NET note (on preceptaustin): the word for "dispute" suggests a legal setting. The hot-headed person is eager to turn every disagreement into a legal case. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary)

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: for the lazy man, every difficulty in his path serves as an excuse for inaction (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Wesley: the righteous man's way is easy and pleasant to him, notwithstanding all its difficulties. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- Pulpit: "the upright" is set against the lazy man because laziness is a serious sin and the opposite of God-fearing hard work (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 20**
- Guzik: a wise son makes his father glad partly because it vindicates the father's trust in God and training of the son in wisdom. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)

**v. 21**
- Matthew Henry: the wicked man sins, not only without regret, but with delight (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_015.cfm).
- Ellicott: folly shows itself in wasted opportunities, and the commission of evil (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 22**
- Guzik: Wisdom understands that other people also have wisdom. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Wesley: plans fail when men do not seek, or will not receive advice from others. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: so much harm is done by the tongue that when a man gives a fitting reply, he can rejoice and treat it as God's gift (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- A writer quoted on preceptaustin: Abigail waited until Nabal was sober before speaking. Job's friends said true things to the wrong man at the wrong time (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).

**v. 24** (does this verse teach life after death?)
- This-life reading: Pulpit says the main sense is that the wise live in a way that keeps them from early death (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm). Ellicott hears a faint echo of Colossians 3:1–2, but says the writer may only have meant long life on earth (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Eternal-life reading: Waltke (on preceptaustin) says "upward," set against the grave below, implies eternal life above and beyond the grave. Preceptaustin itself agrees, while noting that some commentaries take it as longer physical life (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary).
- Wesley applies it spiritually: the wise place his heart, and treasure, and conversation on things above. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)

**v. 25**
- Ellicott: God establishes the landmark of the helpless widow, who has none to cry to but Him. Moving a neighbour's landmark was a common form of oppression (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Wesley: "the proud" are the mighty oppressors, and "the border" means the estate (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/).

**v. 26**
- Guzik: Wickedness doesn't begin with actions; it begins in the heart and thoughts. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/)
- Ellicott reads it differently: "thoughts of evil, wicked designs." Kind, soothing words are pure in God's sight (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: "troubleth his own house" uses the same word as the Achan story (Joshua 7:25). The "gifts" are bribes taken by a judge (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Pulpit: this applies first to an honest judge, and more widely to anyone free of greed. We see here a hope of immortality, to which integrity leads. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm)

**v. 28**
- Wesley: the wicked man speaks from the mouth - Not the heart; for he rashly speaks what comes into his mouth, without the direction of his heart or conscience. (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/)
- Ellicott compares James 3 on the power of words (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).

**v. 29**
- Ellicott: God hears the righteous for they desire above all things to do His will, and so their petitions to this effect are heard by Him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm)

**v. 30**
- Two readings of "the light of the eyes": Ellicott says it does the heart good to see one whose eyes are sparkling with happiness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm). Gill takes it to mean the things seen, such as nature and light itself (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/15-30.htm).
- "Good report": Ellicott says good news. Wesley and Poole say a good name (https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-proverbs/). Gill applies it to the gospel report (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/15-30.htm).

**v. 31**
- Ellicott: this is reproof which leads to life, and "the ear" stands for the whole person (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Matthew Henry: well-received reproofs are a means of spiritual life and lead to eternal life (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_015.cfm).

**v. 32**
- Matthew Henry: people who refuse instruction undervalue their own souls. The fundamental error of sinners is undervaluing their own souls (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_015.cfm).

**v. 33**
- Ellicott: the fear of the Lord is a discipline which leads to wisdom, and humility leads to honour (compare Luke 1:52) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/15.htm).
- Guzik: fearing God means recognising who he is and who we are, and that produces the humility God exalts (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-15/).
- Wiersbe (on preceptaustin): this fear is not the servile fear of the slave before the master but the reverential and respectful fear of the child before the parent. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-15-commentary)
- Pulpit notes an added line in some ancient texts, "Glory goeth before the humble," and links it to Christ in Hebrews 12:2 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/15.htm).
